w: What's tested Who contributed what: Bonwill, Balkwill, von Spee, Bennett, Christensen, Monson, Pankey-Mann-Schuyler, the gnathologists (Stallard and Stuart, D'Amico, P.K. Thomas) PMS vs gnathology: what each assumed, which instruments, what they learned The modern ideas (conformative, gnathology, Pankey/Dawson, bioesthetics, neuromuscular): what they share and how they differ The four modern concepts: posterior support (first), plane of occlusion, occlusal contacts (tripodization vs point to surface, freedom), anterior guidance Shortened dental arch; the custom anterior guide table; Dawson's smile design steps and phonetics Patients rarely look like the ideal dentoform, but "do principles of normal occlusion apply? Yes." The fundamentals came from about 175 years of ideas, first for dentures, then (about a century later) applied to natural teeth, where some didn't work. Where the ideas came from W.G.A. Bonwill, "father of articulation" ca. 1858 Equilateral triangle: about 4 inches (110 mm) condyle to condyle to the mandibular symphysis (from thousands of skulls). Led to the occlusal plane concept and the first scientifically based arrangement: bilaterally balanced occlusion. Articulators still use 110 mm intercondylar widths F.H. Balkwill 1866 The translating condyle moves medially in lateral movement, 40 years before Bennett Count von Spee 1890 The occlusal curve in the sagittal plane I.M. Bromill 1897 Diagrammed facial planes; anatomic landmarks for tooth positions Carl Christensen 1901 Arc of mandibular movement; posterior separation in protrusion; the protrusive record J.B. Parfitt 1902 First to put curved condylar paths on an articulator Norman G. Bennett 1908 Lateral translation of the mandible George Monson ca. 1916 Spherical theory: combined the 4-inch triangle, bilateral balance, Spee's curve and Balkwill's and Christensen's condylar observations into a 4-inch sphere. His instrument did not reproduce the condyles; it used a central rotational center with set screws In the 1800s, a geometric relationship was thought to mean something about function. The 4-inch triangle is real (it still holds on CT scans), but it doesn't dictate how we should function. Still, dentures built on Monson's sphere were generally very successful, and curve-following setups are still used, especially when many teeth are missing. Two schools, 1930s to 1970s Pankey, Mann and Schuyler (PMS) combined Monson's theory with Meyer's functionally generated path (FGP, 1933): the mandibular posteriors were restored to the 4-inch sphere, then the maxillary posteriors were built from an FGP, pathways the patient ground into wax. They argued an instrument reproducing condylar motion was unnecessary because the FGP recorded it, and used a simple suspension articulator with a big base. Applying denture balance to teeth didn't work, so Schuyler evolved the concept: eliminate balancing contacts, elevate anterior guidance, use contact areas rather than point contacts, and adopt simpler instruments (the Hanau H2 semi-adjustable articulator, an arbitrary face-bow and the Broadrick occlusal plane analyzer, a "flag" scribed with a 4-inch arc from the canine and distal molar). Gnathology (from McCollum's work) aimed to replicate the patient exactly: locate the rotational centers of the condyles in all three dimensions, record every border movement with a pantograph, and program a fully adjustable articulator, so restorations made on it would need little adjustment. Early goals: MICP coincident with CR in the rearmost, uppermost, midmost (RUM) position (wrong by today's understanding: "you need a good glass of rum"), and bilateral balance in excursions ("Yikes!"). The gnathologists then contributed lasting ideas: Stallard and Stuart, cuspid protection (canine guidance), keyword disclusion; D'Amico, mutually protected occlusion, keyword force (anterior teeth handle off-axis forces better); Peter K. Thomas, cusp-fossa waxing (your PKT instruments); Niles Guichet, simpler (but still complex) fully adjustable instruments. Gnathology "could rarely be achieved," and its followers blamed the instruments, not the philosophy. Digital jaw tracking (e.g. ModJaw feeding a virtual articulator) has revived its goal of representing the patient. Modern concepts combine both schools, and by the mid-1990s they were pretty well defined. Differing modern ideas Conformative Match what is there; don't change the existing occlusion. About 90-98% of general dentistry, when the patient is healthy and asymptomatic Gnathology Capture the condyles' axes in 3-D; posterior occlusal anatomy should replicate condylar motion Pankey / Dawson From PMS; respects CR (when to use it to diagnose and treat) and elevates anterior guidance as the major controlling factor Bioesthetics Form, function and esthetics are linked; VDO can be set arbitrarily from a fixed interarch measurement; strong anterior vertical overlap allows more esthetic posterior cusps Neuromuscular Jankelson; the LVI. Restore at the "myocentric point" of least muscle activity found with a TENS unit (Myo-Monitor). Requires an increased vertical, i.e. full-mouth rehabilitation, and a more forward position without joint stability; not taught at UAB All have some success, because patients adapt. They agree that all teeth should touch at once and that back teeth shouldn't interfere when the jaw moves. They differ on the maxillomandibular (condylar) relationship, the VDO, and the envelope of function and anterior guidance. Frank Speer: "What a patient does to an occlusion may be more important than the occlusion itself." He asked two questions of any philosophy: can you apply it to all patients, and can you apply it without having to restore teeth? The goals of modern occlusion are the same list as Lec1: stable centric contacts, force down the long axes, no balancing contacts, canine disclusion or anterior group function: mutually protected occlusion, in MIP or CO, laterally and in protrusion. Four modern concepts 1. Posterior support ("building the dance floor"). Usually the first consideration in a restorative plan; anterior guidance follows closely as the second. "Support first, disclusion second." Without posterior teeth the anteriors take all the force and chewing work and decline fast, and the jaw overcloses (posterior overclosure, old term posterior bite collapse), leaving less restorative space. Patients often want their "social six" treated; spending their savings on six anterior crowns without posterior support is doomed. How much support? The shortened dental arch: restoring to the second premolar shows no difference in chewing ability, TMD, tooth migration, periodontal support or comfort; the WHO considers at least 20 natural teeth functional and esthetic. Esthetics may suffer where first molars show. 2. Plane of occlusion. Supraeruption, tilting and rotation, interferences and malocclusion prevent an ideal plane, and a violated plane makes disclusion impossible. Dr. Givan's regretted early case: crowns placed against an extruded opposing molar that interfered in every excursion. Fix the plane first: enameloplasty for about half a millimeter, a crown to shorten more, and sometimes extraction when intentional endo plus crown lengthening (into the furcation) is too much. 3. Occlusal contacts. Replicating occlusal anatomy (cusps, ridges, grooves) matters, matched to the patient (flatter crowns for a flat-cusped bruxer). Tripodization (from gnathology): each cusp tip contacts the opposing fossa on three surfaces, up to 27 contacts across a quadrant; excellent stability, difficult in metal and extremely difficult in porcelain, no wiggle room so it requires immediate disclusion; suggested only when the opposing surfaces are controlled or in full reconstruction. Point to surface (modern): a cusp tip contacts a flat surface, so force goes down the long axis and there is horizontal freedom, especially valuable with an immediate lateral translation; used regardless of the extent of treatment. Move contacts off inclines and give room before anterior disclusion: "freedom in the functional area." Mediolateral freedom lets the immediate lateral translation happen without an interference; anteroposterior freedom allows the slide from the CR contact to MICP, a long centric. 4. Anterior guidance. The most important determinant and the one you control most, through the lingual contours of the maxillary anterior teeth. They must accommodate the functional opening, closing and eccentric pathways, the envelope of function (contact near the cingulum, a flatter zone, then steeper, following the chewing pattern). Without good anterior guidance (anterior open bite, minimal overlap, edge to edge), you rely on condylar guidance, which is far less effective. Gnathologists focused on posterior guidance; modern philosophy sides with Schuyler that anterior guidance matters more. To build it: diagnostic wax-up → provisionals tried in the mouth → capture their pathways in a custom anterior guide table (or scan them digitally) → final crowns follow the same pathways. Dawson's 7-step smile design 1. Centric stops Holding contacts on the lingual of the maxillary anteriors; the contours must still disclude the posteriors 2. Lip support Emergence from the labial gingiva. A gingival bulge is a common lab compensation for an under-prepared tooth; measure the provisionals' thickness 3. Lip closure Unstrained closure; space for guidance; no heavy contact on the lower lip 4. Tooth to lip "F and v should be your friends": incisal edge at the wet-dry line; edges follow the smile line. The provisionals are the real test 5. Lingual contours Verify CR holding contacts, check need for a long centric, smooth protrusive function, decide single vs group lateral guidance for posterior disclusion 6. Cingulum contour Rounded for normal d and t sounds; over-bulked on a tongue-thrust patient = labial tooth movement (but holding contact is vital) 7. Verify with "s" Closest speaking space: too much space = lisp, too little = teeth bump or whistle. Done right, the contours sit within the neutral zone From very "crazy" ideas (they weren't crazy at the time) to 2026: all teeth touching in centric, posteriors discluded in eccentrics, mutually protected occlusion.
